content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
**Summary:**
This paper an EnTranNAS method to reduce the gap between the architectures in search and evaluation. To accelerate the search process, the authors further propose a feature sharing strategy. This paper is well-written. However, the importance of the considered problem since it may not necessarily appear in all NAS methods.

**Strengths:**
1. The authors propose a new method to reduce the gap between the architectures in search and evaluation for gradient-based NAS methods.
2. The authors propose a new search space that consists of Engine-cells and Transit-cells.

**Weaknesses:**
1. The results on ImageNet are not very promising. Most NAS methods follow the mobile setting where the number of multiply-add operations (MAdds) in the model is restricted to be less than 600M on ImageNet. However, the best searched architecture has much more MAdds than the constraint. More critically, the searched architecture that satisfies this constraint yields lower accuracy than existing methods, e.g., PCDARTS. 
2. The scope of the considered problem is very limited. The gap of the architectures between search and evaluation only appears in gradient-based methods, e.g., DARTS. As for those reinforcement learning based methods, e.g., ENAS, both the search and evaluation phases train a single sub-graph. Thus, there seems no gap of the architectures between search and evaluation for these methods.
3. The authors argue that “feature sharing strategy is introduced for more efficient parameter training”. However, it is not clear why the feature sharing strategy is able to accelerate the search process. More discussions should be provided.
4. The proposed method uses a different search space from DARTS. Thus, it is hard to judge whether the performance improvement comes from the proposed search method or the changed search space. Ablation studies should be provided.
5. The assumption “the same operation from node i to other nodes j > i always shares the same feature in one cell” is questionable, since the parameters of these operations may be different. Are there any experiments to verify this argument? More discussions should be provided.
6. It is not clear why the proposed method has to perform normalization using Eqn. (7). The motivation should be clarified.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer's effort on reviewing our paper. We offer our responses to the reviewer’s questions and concerns as follows:

-	1. Concern that the results on ImageNet have large FLOPs.

Admittedly, we did not manually restrict the FLOPs of searched architectures to be less than 600M, which causes the fact that the best result on ImageNet (EnTranNAS-DST) has much more FLOPs. However, the best result is mainly used to explore for a higher performance when breaking the limitation of topology. So the FLOPs inevitably increase. As we don't want our searched architecture suffer from a fixed topology (each node only has two input connections), accordingly, it should not be restricted by a limited FLOPs. 

We need to point out that our true contribution is that we have opened a door to topology search in the DARTS space, and have presented a methodology to extend the flexibility of search results while significantly reducing the search cost, instead of solely targeting at an architecture with lower FLOPs. It should not be valid to deny our contributions just because we have one search result with larger FLOPs than 600M. Besides, our result of EnTranNAS (ImageNet) has similar number of FLOPs to the one of PC-DARTS (637M v.s. 597M), but achieves nearly the same performance (24.3%/7.2% v.s. 24.2%/7.3%) with only a half of the search cost of PC-DARTS (1.9day v.s. 3.8day). So we do not think that 40M more FLOPs are significant enough to deny our contribution of the obvious advantage on search cost. 

-	2. Concern that the scope of the considered problem is limited. 

We have to say that the reviewer’s concern about the scope we focus on is overcritical and unfair. The neural architecture search literature can be categorized into multiple streams, such as reinforcement learning based methods, evolution based methods, and gradient based methods. They have different properties with respect to search cost, search space, and enjoy different advantages and suffer from different problems. Our study belongs to the gradient based studies and focuses on an important and unsolved problem existed in the gradient based methods. As mentioned by AnonReviewer 1, some gradient based studies, such as P-DARTS and DrNAS etc, also tackle the same issue. These studies would be insignificant if the reviewer’s criterion is adopted. We guess that the reviewer might be more interested in reinforcement learning based methods, but it is overcritical and unfair to deny our gradient based study by the fact that the problems we focus on do not appear in reinforcement learning based methods. 

-	3. Question: why the feature sharing strategy is able to accelerate?

The same operation from node $i$ to node $j>i$ share the same feature in the same cell. As a result, the feature of one operation from the node $i$ is calculated only once and are re-used for later nodes $j>i$, which saves much computation and accelerates the search. For any operation, a cell with $n$ nodes needs to perform the operation for 1+2+…+($n$-1) times without the feature sharing strategy, but only ($n$-1) times with the strategy enabled. 

-	4. Concern that search space is different from DARTS.

We have done fair comparison using the standard and extended search spaces, respectively. As shown in Table 6, the standard search space is exactly the same as that of DARTS. Since our method is friendly to memory cost, we are able to search with more operations and make an extended search space containing 12 operations. In Table 4, the methods without the notation “(12 operations)” adopt the same standard search space. They are compared together for fair comparison. We compare our method in the extended search space with NASP that also adopts 12 operations. So we have eliminated the effects of search space in comparison. 

-	5. Question: experiments to verify the assumption?

It is correct that the parameters of these operations that share the same feature may be different. However, it only impedes the representation ability of the super-net, but does not affect the search process. Note that the original super-net and the super-net with the feature sharing strategy offer the same operations on the same nodes for us to search. So the two search processes are equivalent. We can use this simplification because what we search for is which operation performed on which node, rather than their parameters. 

The reviewer may be confused by the word “assuming”. Our intension is not to assume that the condition (the same operation from node i to other nodes j > i always shares the same feature in one cell) is true. The condition is hard to be satisfied because the parameters may be different as mentioned by the reviewer. Our actual intension is to make this simplification. We hereby clarify that the word “assuming” should be replaced with “simplifying”.

content.title: question 6
content.comment:
-	6. Question: why the normalization has to be performed?

Because we want to enable differentiable sparsification and break the topology limitation, we need to cut out connections for each intermediate node, instead of each edge. Given that there should be at least one connection kept for each intermediate node, we perform the max normalization for the probabilities $p^{(i,j)}_k$ that direct to the same node $j$, in order to make them relatively comparable and restricted to [0,1]. Then we can make thresholding for these normalized logits, and so the differentiable sparsification is realized.

content.title: Motivation behind the approach is good, but the novelty part is not that significant
content.review:
This paper proposes a method for reducing the gap between the search and final evaluation phases in differentiable architecture search.

Contributions:
- This paper introduces a modification to the cell-based architecture search via gradient-based methods such as DARTS [1] by modifying the search space in order to enable sparse architectural weighs and therefore more efficient computation and lower memory consumption during the search.
- The results on the standard CIFAR-10 and ImageNet benchmarks are competitive.

Detailed comments:
Despite the motivation behind the proposed approach is plausible, I think the contributions of this paper are incremental considering the myriad of follow-up papers of DARTS [1], some of them also considering to tackle the same issue as in this paper [2, 3]. The proposed approach seems useful from an engineering perspective, since it results in lower search runtimes and memory costs, however the methodological contributions are not enough. Moreover, there are some research questions which are not answered throughout the paper like these one: 
- How is the performance of the final architecture retrained from scratch correlated with the one-shot performance or the perfomance of the same architecture evaluated with the one-shot weights?
- How sensitive is the search towards search hyperparamters such as the softmax temperature (how did you tune it in the first place?) or the \lambda in equation (11)?

Considering the aforementioned concerns, I am leaning towards a reject.

Other:
The related work section is well-written, however some important references are missing such as the works that study the performance gap between search and final evaluation [4, 5] or the DNW paper [6].

[1] Hanxiao Liu,  Karen Simonyan,  and Yiming Yang.   Darts:  Differentiable architecture search.   In ICLR 2019
[2] Xin Chen, Lingxi Xie, Jun Wu, and Qi Tian. Progressive differentiable architecture search: Bridgingthe depth gap between search and evaluation. In ICCV 2020
[3] Xiangning Chen, Ruochen Wang, Minhao Cheng, Xiaocheng Tang, Cho-Jui Hsieh. DrNAS: Dirichlet Neural Architecture Search. In ArXiv 2020
[4] Arber Zela, Thomas Elsken, Tonmoy Saikia, Yassine Marrakchi, Thomas Brox, and Frank Hutter.  Understanding and robustifying differentiable architecture search. In ICLR 2020
[5] Xiangning Chen and Cho-Jui Hsieh. Stabilizing differentiable architecture search via perturbation-based regularization. In ICML 2020
[6] Mitchell Wortsman, Ali Farhadi, Mohammad Rastegari. Discovering Neural Wirings. In NeurIPS 2019
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer's effort on reviewing our paper.  We offer our responses to the reviewer’s questions and concerns as follows:

- Question 1: the correlation between the retrained architecture and one-shot performance. 

In our paper, we follow SNAS [1] and use the performance drop of the super-net after architecture derivation to reflect the correlation of the architectures in search and evaluation, as shown in Table1 in our paper. We think it is also a good suggestion to directly measure the correlation of the retrained performance and the one-shot performance. We adopt the Kendall metric [2] that evaluates the rank correlation of data pairs. It ranges from -1 to 1 as the ranking order changes from being reversed to identical. We run DARTS, P-DARTS, PC-DARTS, EnTranNAS and EnTranNAS-DST on CIFAR-10 for 6 times with different seeds, and retrain these searched architectures. We calculate the Kendall metric for each method using the six retrained accuracies in evaluation and the six one-shot accuracies in search. Their comparisons are as follows:

Method            Kendall $\tau$

DARTS             -0.47 (-7/15)

P-DARTS          0.2 (3/15)

PC-DARTS	  -0.07 (-1/15)

EnTranNAS	  0.33 (5/15)

EnTranNAS-DST    0.6 (9/15)

It is shown that EnTranNAS and EnTranNAS-DST have the top-2 Kendall scores, which indicates that our methods help to improve the correlation of architecture performances in search and evaluation. 

We hope this result, together with the Table 1 in our paper, could answer the reviewer’s question. 

- Question 2: the sensitivity of hyper-parameters, such as the temperature and the $\lambda$.

Our methods have two hyper-parameters, the temperature in Eq. (5) and the $\lambda$ in Eq. (11). As for the $\lambda$, we have done ablation studies for it in the Table 3 in our paper. 

Actually, both the $\lambda$ and the temperature have the same role of controlling the capacities of the searched architecture. If the temperature has a higher initial value, there would be more connections kept in the finally converged architecture, because our method cut out connections when their distribution is sharp (see Eq. (7-8) in our paper). If the temperature is large, the distribution of $p^{(i,j)}_k$ would be flat, and $\hat{p}^{(i,j)}_k$ would be large by Eq (7), so more connections would be kept by Eq. (8). 

Since the $\lambda$ and the temperature have the same role, we fix the setting of temperature and leave the $\lambda$ as a tunable variable, just like the factor of a regularizer, to control the architecture capacity. We set the temperature following [3] where the temperature is initialized as 5.0 and is annealed down by a factor every epoch. Other settings of the temperature would also be feasible but the effect of $\lambda$ on the architecture capacity would be different accordingly. 

So it is not tricky to tune these hyper-parameters. When the setting of temperature is fixed in any manner, practitioners can easily control the architecture capacity by choosing a proper $\lambda$. 

- Concern 1: the contributions are incremental. 

We respectfully disagree with the reviewer. We do not think it reasonable to deny the contribution of one paper just because there have been many follow-up papers focusing on the same issue. Our design of Engine and Transit cell, feature sharing strategy, and the method to support differentiable sparsification are novel and have enough contents to be a significant work. Our study, P-DARTS, and DrNAS tackle the similar issue, but propose different methods. If the reviewer denies our novelty, it will be more appropriate to enumerate the similarity between our methods and the existing literature. 

- Concern 2: the methodological contributions are not enough. 

Again, we respectfully disagree with the reviewer. The reviewer claims that our methodological contributions are not enough but unfortunately does not demonstrate with any evidence or explanation. So we think it unfair. Admittedly, the design of Engine and Transit cells are derived from an empirical methodology. However it is reasonable and in line with intuitions. Its validity is also confirmed by experiments. 

Actually, many accepted studies in the same area are proposed by empirical methodology. For example, P-DARTS gradually shrinks the number of operations and extends the depth. PC-DARTS only feeds a small portion of channels into each candidate operation. They are all empirical designs but one cannot deny their contributions. Therefore, it is unfair to deny our methodological contributions just because some of our designs are derived in an empirical way. 

[1] S. Xie, et al., Snas: stochastic neural architecture search. In ICLR, 2019.
[2] M. G. Kendall. A new measure of rank correlation. Biometrika, 30(1/2):81–93, 1938
[3] Bichen Wu, et al.,.Fbnet: Hardware-aware efficient convnet design via differentiable neural architecture search. In CVPR, 2019.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
The paper proposes EnTranNAS to reduce the gap between the search and evaluation in cell-based NAS. Specifically, it builds the super-net with engine-cells and transit-cells. Engine-cell keeps the whole DAG (same as the cell in DARTS) while transit cell only keeps the currently active sub-graph. A feature sharing technique is proposed to alleviate uneven optimization on candidate operations. It also introduces an architecture derivation method to further reduce the gap between engine-cells and derived-cells. 

Pros:
1. The idea of building the super-net with two different types of cells (engine-cell that keeps the full DAG, transit-cell that only keeps the active sub-graph) is interesting and novel for cell-based NAS. 

2. The proposed method achieves good results on CIFAR-10 (similar or higher accuracy while having lower search cost). 
	
Cons:
1. Experiment results on ImageNet are a bit confusing. EnTranNAS-DST gives higher accuracy but also has higher #FLOPs than the baseline models, making the comparisons confusing. I suggest adding a figure showing the trade-off curve (accuracy-FLOPs) of the searched neural network architecture by adjusting the width multiplier or input resolution. 

2. Table 2 only shows the efficiency effect of each component. It would be interesting to add accuracy results to show the accuracy effect of each component in Table 2.  

Overall, I think the proposed method is novel for cell-based NAS. But I also find the empirical results are a bit weak and confusing. Therefore, I recommend "Marginally above acceptance threshold".
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer's effort on reviewing our paper. We offer our responses to the reviewer’s questions and concerns as follows:

-	Concern about the FLOPs.

As mentioned in our response to AnonReviewer3, we do not limit the search result under the mobile setting considering our searched architectures support flexible topologies. We intend to search for architectures with variant scales and explore the best result that can be achieved by the DARTS-based space, so the best result inevitably has higher FLOPs than the baseline methods. Besides, our experiments on CIFAR-10 have demonstrated the effectiveness of both EnTranNAS and EnTranNAS-DST. All experiments are conducted in the same settings, including width multiplier and input resolution, for fair comparison. 

-	Concern about the accuracy effect of each component. 

Thanks for the reviewer’s suggestion. We will consider making a comparison of the accuracy effects of these components in the later version of our paper.

content.title: An interesting work towards differential NAS
content.review:
The authors introduced EnTranNAS and EnTranNAS-DST, tailored for the handling gap architectures search and evaluation. Results on large-scale datasets such as ImageNet confirm the validity.

Strength:
1. The overall idea is quite interesting. By introducing some parameters to support differentiable sparsification, the architecture search turns out equivalent to that by choosing the non-zero connections. 
2. Experimental results are promising. The proposed EnTranNAS-DST showcases good results, proving the effectiveness of the differentiable search. Moreover, searching with additional operations doesn't seem to scale up the cost.
3. The submission is generally well organized and easy to follow.

Weakness:
1. Is there any quantitative analysis of the reduced gap? It is observed that the accuracy drop is decreased in Tab.1, yet still, it doesn't necessarily mean that the architecture gap is reduced. An apparent example is that, in the first configuration, the performance drop is smaller than that of the last one, but the architecture gap between the two appears to be the same. Try to use some other metrics for evaluations.

2. It would be great if more theoretical analysis, at least some formulations, are provided as the foundation of the design. The current design appears somehow ad-hoc.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

replying_to: Replying to An interesting work towards differential NAS

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer's effort on reviewing our paper. We offer our responses to the reviewer’s questions and concerns as follows:

-	Other metric to evaluate the reduced gap. 

Thanks for the reviewer’s suggestion. As mentioned in our response to AnonReviewer1, we use the Kendall metric to measure the correlation between search and evaluation, which reflects the reduced gap. It is shown that our proposed methods enjoy the best Kendall $\tau$ scores and improve the correlation. The result also indicates that our methods work to reduce the architecture gap. 

-	More theoretical analysis.

Thanks for the reviewer’s suggestion. The Engine & Transit cell design is introduced in a somewhat empirical manner. But actually it is just a part of our proposed methods and serves as the basis of EnTranNAS-DST that has more rigid analysis and formulations. We will consider having more theoretical analysis for some of the empirical designs in the later version of our paper.
